title: The Blank Cheque: a Hamburg Banker from the Ferdinandstraße to Sleepy Hollow
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Hamburg, born into the banking house
stops.date_confidence: attested; the German and English Wikipedia articles and deutsche-biographie agree on 5 June 1867. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the family birth-house pin already fixed for his brother Aby's birth; de.wiki gives the family's address that year as Grindelhof 1a, which geocodes some 400 m from that pin.
stops.campa: Max Moritz Warburg is born in the Grindel quarter of Hamburg on the fifth of June, one of seven children of Moritz Warburg and Charlotte Oppenheim. The eldest son is expected to take the firm, and Max is not the eldest; Aby, born the year before, is the one the counting room is waiting for. The house is a banking house before it is anything else. M. M. Warburg & Co., in business since 1798, moves this same year into Ferdinandstraße 75, and has not left that address since.
suggested_refs: The Grindel quarter of Hamburg, called Little Jerusalem, where the family lived at Max's birth

stops.name: Mittelweg 17, the villa at the Johnsallee
stops.date_confidence: attested; de.wiki dates the move to 1871 and gives the address as Mittelweg 17 at the corner of the Johnsallee. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinates corrected to the Nominatim geocode for Mittelweg 17; the research pool's longitude was roughly 410 m west, and its record carried a malformed duplicate key for the same field.
stops.campa: Four years after his birth the family leaves the Grindel for a villa at Mittelweg 17, on the corner of the Johnsallee. The Grindel is where Hamburg's Jews live thickly enough that the city calls the quarter Little Jerusalem; the Mittelweg is where its merchants live. Moritz Warburg moves his household across that line and drops none of his ties to the congregation on the other side of it. The sons are raised orthodox in observance at an address that is Hanseatic, a few minutes' walk from the Außenalster and the houses of the shipping families.
suggested_refs: The Warburg villa at Mittelweg 17, Rotherbaum

stops.name: Hamburg, the birthright bought for books
stops.date_confidence: traditional [R]; the exchange survives only as Max Warburg's own recollection, written down decades later and printed by Gombrich, not as any document. The year follows the ages he gives, thirteen and twelve. Month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the existing family pin, which the aby_warburg file already uses for the same scene.
stops.campa: Aby is thirteen, Max twelve. The elder brother offers the younger his birthright: the firm, the partnership, the whole future of the house. Not for a mess of pottage. For a standing undertaking that Max will buy him every book he ever needs. Max agrees. He keeps it for fifty years, through Florence, through the Kreuzlingen clinic, through the library on the Heilwigstraße that swallows a bank partner's income year after year. He calls it afterwards the biggest blank cheque of his life.
stops.quote: Als er dreizehn Jahr alt war, offerierte er mir sein Erstgeborenenrecht. Er als Ältester war bestimmt, in die Firma einzutreten. Ich war damals zwölf Jahre, noch nicht sehr überlegungsreif und erklärte mich einverstanden, ihm das Erstgeborenenrecht abzukaufen. Er offerierte es mir aber nicht für ein Linsengericht, sondern verlangte von mir eine Zusage, daß ich ihm immer alle Bücher kaufen würde, die er brauchte.
stops.quote_source: Max Warburg's own recollection, quoted in Ernst H. Gombrich, 'Aby Warburg' (Neuausgabe, Hamburg 2006), reproduced with citation in the German Wikipedia article 'Aby Warburg'
suggested_refs: Ernst H. Gombrich, 'Aby Warburg: An Intellectual Biography', on the birthright anecdote
sources: Karen Michels, 'Es muss besser werden!' (Hamburg University Press, 2020)

stops.name: Speersort, the Abitur at the Johanneum
stops.date_confidence: attested; de.wiki records the Abitur at the Realgymnasium of the Gelehrtenschule des Johanneums in 1886. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinates are the school's Speersort site in the Altstadt, occupied until its 1914 move to Winterhude; the pair carried in the research pool matches neither address.
stops.campa: He finishes at the Realgymnasium of the Gelehrtenschule des Johanneums, then standing at the Speersort in the Altstadt, and takes his Abitur. That is the end of his formal education: no university follows it, and the only degree he will ever hold is an honorary one, given to him at fifty-four. He is eighteen. The man who will spend thirty years on the boards of German banking, shipping and monetary policy learns the rest of it at four desks in four countries, starting that autumn at a private bank in Frankfurt.
suggested_refs: The Gelehrtenschule des Johanneums at the Speersort, Hamburg Altstadt, before the 1914 move to Maria-Louisen-Straße

stops.name: Frankfurt, apprenticed at J. Dreyfus & Co.
stops.date_confidence: attested; de.wiki and deutsche-biographie both place the apprenticeship at J. Dreyfus & Co. in Frankfurt from 1886, running about two years. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. The firm's 1880s address was not located; coordinates are central Frankfurt.
stops.campa: The training is deliberate and it is foreign. Warburg is put to a two-year apprenticeship at J. Dreyfus & Co. in Frankfurt, a Jewish private bank of the older kind, and learns acceptance credit, bills, and the discipline of a house that lives on its name and can be ruined by a rumour. Hamburg is a trading city and its banks finance cargo. Frankfurt is a lending city and its banks finance states, and nobody explains to him that he is being taught to work in both. He is nineteen when he starts and twenty-one when he leaves.
suggested_refs: The private banking house J. Dreyfus & Co., Frankfurt am Main

stops.name: Amsterdam, the desk at Wertheim & Gompertz
stops.date_confidence: the Amsterdam stage is confirmed in general terms by deutsche-biographie; de.wiki names Wertheim & Gompertz and the year 1888 [A]. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinates are central Amsterdam, the firm's address not located.
stops.campa: From Frankfurt to Amsterdam, and a trainee's place at Wertheim & Gompertz. The Dutch house deals in colonial produce and in the foreign exchange that moves it, in a city whose bourse is older than every bank in Germany. He is twenty and the youngest man at his table. The year teaches him to read a bill drawn in one currency, accepted in a second and payable in a third, and to price it in the time it takes to set the paper back down on the table in front of him.
suggested_refs: Wertheim & Gompertz, Amsterdam, and the Dutch acceptance trade of the 1880s

stops.name: Munich, the year with the Chevaulegers
stops.date_confidence: the military service of 1888 to 1890 is confirmed by deutsche-biographie; de.wiki names the III Royal Bavarian Chevaulegers and the rank of Vizefeldwebel [A]. Month from the research pool's October 1888, day defaulted to 01. The antisemitism read on the blocked commission is a widely repeated biographical interpretation and not a documented decision [R].
stops.campa: He interrupts the banking years for the one-year volunteer term, in the Third Royal Bavarian Chevaulegers, a light cavalry regiment. He rides well and rises to Vizefeldwebel, and the regiment puts him up as an officer candidate. The commission does not come. Every account of his life gives the same reason, and not one of them produces the order that would prove it. Was he refused for being a Jew, or passed over for something the file no longer holds? He serves out the year, hands back the horse, and goes on to Paris without an answer.
suggested_refs: The III Royal Bavarian Chevaulegers Regiment, Munich, and the Einjährig-Freiwilliger system

stops.name: Paris, the Banque Impériale Ottomane
stops.date_confidence: traditional [R]; the Paris stage at the Banque Impériale Ottomane and the unenrolled Sorbonne attendance come from de.wiki and the biographical literature, not from a document reachable this session. Year 1890, month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinates are the central Paris banking district; the branch address was not located.
stops.campa: Paris, and a place at the Banque Impériale Ottomane, the Anglo-French house that serves the Ottoman state as its bank and its debt manager. Here the paper is sovereign: tribute revenues, railway concessions, the loans of an empire that borrows faster than it collects. In the evenings he goes to the Sorbonne and sits in on lectures without enrolling for anything, which is how he takes most of his education. He is twenty-three and has now watched a government financed from outside itself.
suggested_refs: The Paris seat of the Banque Impériale Ottomane and its management of Ottoman sovereign debt
sources: Gabriele Hoffmann, 'Max M. Warburg' (Hamburg 2009), via the research dossier

stops.name: New Court, the last placement
stops.date_confidence: attested; deutsche-biographie places him at N. M. Rothschild & Sons in London by 1891, and the placement runs into 1892. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the existing New Court pin in St Swithin's Lane.
stops.campa: The last placement is New Court in St Swithin's Lane, the London house that Mayer Amschel Rothschild's fifth son planted in the City eighty years before Warburg walks into it. Sterling is the world's money and this is one of the rooms where it is lent. He is twenty-four. He has now worked in Frankfurt, Amsterdam, Paris and London, holds no degree in anything, and speaks the four languages in which the century's money is counted. The training is finished.
suggested_refs: N. M. Rothschild & Sons at New Court, St Swithin's Lane, London

stops.name: Ferdinandstraße 75, made a personally liable partner
stops.date_confidence: attested; mmwarburg.de and deutsche-biographie both give 1893 for the partnership. Month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinates corrected to the Nominatim geocode of Ferdinandstraße 75; the pair 53.5493, 10.0007, repeated on six separate entries in the research pool, lies about 400 m south-east in the wrong block.
stops.campa: He comes home to Hamburg at twenty-six and is made a personally liable partner of M. M. Warburg & Co. Personally liable is not a formula. The partners answer for the house with everything they own, and the house has answered that way since 1798. His father Moritz still runs it. His brother Paul becomes a partner two years later and leaves for New York and Kuhn, Loeb, carrying the family's American half with him. Max works out of the Ferdinandstraße from 1893 until May 1938.
suggested_refs: M. M. Warburg & Co., Ferdinandstraße 75, Hamburg, in business at that address since 1867

stops.name: Table Bay, the voyage south
stops.date_confidence: traditional [R]; the voyage, the illness and the inland mine inspection come from Gabriele Hoffmann's biography and from Warburg's own memoir 'Aus meinen Aufzeichnungen' (1952), and are undated in every reachable source. The year given here is an ordering device for the segment and not a claim; it is placed before the 1899 marriage only to keep the segment monotonic. The Swaziland tin district is placed at approximate coordinates near Forbes Reef, -26.05, 31.15.
stops.campa: A business voyage takes him to the Cape to look at South African trade, and it nearly kills him. He contracts a severe dysentery and loses something like twenty kilograms, the only serious illness his biographers record before old age. When he can stand again he goes inland with an engineer to inspect a tin mine in the Swaziland hills, several hundred miles from the nearest bank. The sources do not say whether the mine was bought, or what he thought of the country.
suggested_refs: Max M. Warburg, 'Aus meinen Aufzeichnungen' (1952), the memoir carrying the South African episode
The Forbes Reef tin workings of the Swaziland mineral belt
sources: Gabriele Hoffmann, 'Max M. Warburg' (Hamburg 2009), via the research dossier

stops.name: Kösterberg, the marriage and the Elbe slope
stops.date_confidence: the 1899 marriage to Alice Magnus is attested by both Wikipedia articles; month and day defaulted to 01. de.wiki dates the couple's residence at Kösterberg to 1899-1907 and their move to a villa on the Alsterufer near the Dammtor to 1907; the family kept the property after moving. Coordinates corrected to the Nominatim geocode for Kösterbergstraße, Blankenese.
stops.campa: He marries Alice Magnus, daughter of Hermann Levin Magnus, and the couple take the Kösterberg property above the Elbe at Blankenese, where the river widens toward the sea and Hamburg's shipowners keep their houses. They live there until 1907, when they move to a villa on the Alsterufer near the Dammtor, closer to the bank. The family keeps the Kösterberg after the move. From the terrace the river is a mile across and full of outbound traffic, and the children are brought up within sight of it.
suggested_refs: The Warburg estate at Kösterberg, Blankenese, above the Elbe

stops.name: Adolphsplatz, the Chamber of Commerce
stops.date_confidence: the 1902 election to the Handelskammer is attested by de.wiki; month and day defaulted to 01. dasjuedischehamburg gives the range 1903-1933, a year late at the front. The seat on the board of the Zentralverband des Deutschen Bank- und Bankiersgewerbes is dated by de.wiki both to 1902 and to 1903; the contradiction is recorded and left standing.
stops.campa: He is elected to the Hamburg Chamber of Commerce, which in this city is not a lobby but a governing body. It sits at the Adolphsplatz beside the exchange and it speaks for the port. He holds the seat for thirty-one years, until the National Socialist administration clears every Jewish member out of it in 1933. In the same season he is put on the board of the German banking trade's central association. The reference works give two different years for that appointment, 1902 and 1903, and neither of them is checked against the other.
suggested_refs: The Hamburg Handelskammer at the Adolphsplatz, and its 1927 gold medal awarded to Warburg

stops.name: Hamburg Rathaus, the seat in the Bürgerschaft
stops.date_confidence: attested; de.wiki gives the Bürgerschaft election to February 1903 for the National Liberal Party, and the appointment as Handelsrichter by the Hamburg Senate to 1897 for a five-year term. Day unknown, defaulted to 01. The securities-exchange board seat is dated 1903 by de.wiki, in the same entry as the disputed Zentralverband appointment.
stops.campa: In February he is elected to the Bürgerschaft, Hamburg's city parliament, for the National Liberals, the party of the merchant bourgeoisie and the fleet. He has been a commercial judge since 1897, appointed by the Senate for a five-year term, and he now sits on the board that governs the securities exchange as well. The banking is one career and the civic office is another. In a city-state this size they are conducted in buildings four streets apart, by the same two hundred men.
suggested_refs: The Hamburg Bürgerschaft in the Rathaus, and the National Liberal representation of the merchant houses

stops.name: Cuxhaven, the deep-sea fishing company
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1908 by de.wiki and corroborated in the dossier's citation of the NDB; month and day defaulted to 01. The further claim that the company became Germany's leading fish supplier by turnover rests on secondary biographical accounts and was not checked against trade data [R].
stops.campa: With Albert Ballin, who runs the Hamburg-Amerika Line and is the nearest thing Warburg has to a working partner outside his own firm, he founds the Cuxhavener Hochseefischerei at the mouth of the Elbe. It means trawlers, ice, a fish market and a rail line to the inland cities, and it means bank money in all of them. The Hamburg way of banking is to own a piece of the thing the money moves. Over the next twenty years he takes board seats in shipping, shipbuilding, colonial trade and fish.
suggested_refs: The Cuxhavener Hochseefischerei AG and the deep-sea fishing harbour at Cuxhaven
sources: Neue Deutsche Biographie, via the research dossier

stops.name: Berlin, the exchange committee
stops.date_confidence: attested; de.wiki records the 1908 seat on the Berliner Börsenausschuss in the Reichsamt des Innern. Month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinates are the Reichsbank complex at Jägerstraße. A 1919 appointment to the Reichsbank Zentralausschuss appears in the research pool but is recorded by neither de.wiki nor deutsche-biographie and is carried here as unverified [R].
stops.campa: He has been, since 1903, an occasional financial adviser to Wilhelm II, which in that court's practice means being asked things at lunch and not being sent for afterwards. Now he is made a member of the stock exchange committee attached to the Imperial Interior Office in Berlin, and takes up the campaign that occupies him for the next several years: revision of the imperial exchange law, which Hamburg's traders regard as agrarian politics wearing the clothes of morality. He is forty-one.
suggested_refs: The Berliner Börsenausschuss in the Reichsamt des Innern, and the campaign to revise the imperial exchange law

stops.name: Ferdinandstraße 75, his father's death
stops.date_confidence: attested; de.wiki and deutsche-biographie both place Moritz Warburg's death in 1910 and Max's sole leadership of the firm from that year. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinates carry the Ferdinandstraße 75 correction described at the 1893 stop.
stops.campa: Moritz Warburg dies and Max, forty-three, becomes head of the house in fact as well as in name. This is the succession his brother sold him for a library thirty-one years before. From this year he leads M. M. Warburg & Co. alone: the balance sheet, the partners, the correspondent network running through Paul in New York into Kuhn, Loeb and through the Hamburg port into every trade that crosses it. The firm is a private partnership with no shareholders and no published accounts.
suggested_refs: The succession at M. M. Warburg & Co. on Moritz Warburg's death, 1910

stops.name: Ballindamm, the HAPAG board
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1910 by de.wiki as to the HAPAG supervisory board and the Hamburg board of the Deutsche Kolonialgesellschaft; month and day defaulted to 01. The Blohm und Voss supervisory seat comes from the dossier's citation of the NDB and was not independently confirmed this session [R].
stops.campa: He joins the supervisory board of the Hamburg-Amerikanische Packetfahrt-Actien-Gesellschaft, whose director Albert Ballin has made it the largest shipping company on earth and whose financing has run through the Warburg bank for years. The same season brings him the Hamburg board of the Deutsche Kolonialgesellschaft and, by Ballin's arrangement, the shipyard Blohm und Voss across the water at Steinwerder, where the hulls go down the ways into the Elbe a few hundred metres from the offices of the men who financed them.
suggested_refs: The HAPAG headquarters on the Ballindamm, Hamburg
The Blohm und Voss yard at Steinwerder
sources: Neue Deutsche Biographie, via the research dossier

stops.name: Kiel, the lunch at Kiel Week
stops.date_confidence: traditional [R]; the Kiel Week exchange survives only in Warburg's own posthumously printed notes, 'Aus meinen Aufzeichnungen' (1952), and in a Welt account of the episode that could not be fetched this session. Kiel Week fell in June 1914, before the Sarajevo assassination on 28 June; day defaulted to 01. The Anglo-German bank venture with Lord Milner is attested for June 1914 by de.wiki.
stops.campa: At a lunch during Kiel Week the Kaiser puts a question to the banker: whether Germany should strike now, before Russian rearmament makes a later war worse. Warburg, by his own account written down long afterwards, urges waiting. It is his account and nobody else's, and what it establishes is access rather than influence. In the same weeks, with Lord Milner, he is setting up an Anglo-German bank in London, on the assumption that the two countries have years of business ahead of them.
suggested_refs: Max M. Warburg, 'Aus meinen Aufzeichnungen' (1952), source of the Kiel Week recollection
sources: Gabriele Hoffmann, 'Max M. Warburg', via the research dossier

segments.name: The War and the Peace That Was Not One

stops.name: Berlin, the War Food Office
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1915 as to the advisory board of the Kriegsernährungsamt by de.wiki; month and day defaulted to 01. The Reichseinkauf initiative with Ballin comes from the dossier's citation of the NDB [R]. The antisemitic profiteering allegations that followed are documented as allegations; the research pool records that the documentary record does not support them.
stops.campa: The British blockade is working and Germany is short of food. Warburg and Ballin promote the Reichseinkauf, a central purchasing body to buy abroad through neutral intermediaries, which the state absorbs as the Zentral-Einkaufsgesellschaft, and Warburg is appointed to the advisory board of the War Food Office. Two Jewish businessmen from Hamburg are now buying the country's bread. The profiteering charge arrives within the year. Nothing in the documentary record supports it, then or since.
suggested_refs: The Kriegsernährungsamt and the Zentral-Einkaufsgesellschaft, Berlin, 1915
sources: Neue Deutsche Biographie, via the research dossier

stops.name: Berlin, the census of Jewish soldiers
stops.date_confidence: the Judenzählung ordered by the Prussian War Ministry in October 1916 is attested by the Deutsches Historisches Museum; month and day defaulted to 01 rather than to the attested October, since Warburg's own dated involvement is not established. His role in the protests comes from the dossier's synthesis of the NDB and was not independently confirmed [R].
stops.campa: The Prussian War Ministry orders a census of the Jews in uniform, to establish how many of them are avoiding the front. It is the first time since emancipation that the German state counts its Jews as Jews, and it counts them while they are dying at Verdun. Warburg, a cavalry volunteer whose own commission was refused, joins the Jewish organizations protesting the order. The count is taken in October. Its findings are never published, and no source reachable now says what they were.
suggested_refs: The Judenzählung of October 1916, ordered by the Prussian War Ministry
sources: Neue Deutsche Biographie, via the research dossier

stops.name: Berlin, the ministry refused
stops.date_confidence: the appointment as financial adviser to Chancellor Prince Max von Baden in October 1918 is documented; day defaulted to 01. The offer of the Reich finance ministry and Warburg's stated reason for declining it come through the NDB and Kopper as biographical interpretation of his own reasoning [R].
stops.campa: In the last weeks of the war Prince Max von Baden, chancellor for thirty-four days, appoints Warburg a financial adviser and offers him the Reich finance ministry. Warburg declines. The reason his biographers give is the one he gave: a Jewish finance minister signing for the terms that are coming would hand the legend its first exhibit. Four weeks later the empire is gone, the sailors have risen at Kiel, and Hamburg is governed by a workers' council.
suggested_refs: The Reich Chancellery under Prince Max von Baden, October 1918
sources: Neue Deutsche Biographie, via the research dossier
Christopher Kopper, on Warburg, via the research dossier

stops.name: Berlin, the delegation he refuses to lead
stops.date_confidence: attested; de.wiki gives the appointment of 12 March 1919, the refusal of the senior role and the recommendation of Carl Melchior, and Warburg's own attendance as an economic and financial expert. en.wiki confirms Melchior's advisory role at the Paris Peace Conference. Coordinates are central Berlin.
stops.campa: He is appointed to the German peace delegation on the twelfth of March and declines the senior place at once, recommending in his stead his own partner Carl Melchior, who takes it. The calculation is the one he made in October: the terms will be unpayable, and the signature under them will be hated for a generation. Melchior, a partner in the same house and a Jew in the same city, accepts the place regardless. Warburg travels to Versailles as an economic and financial expert.
suggested_refs: Carl Melchior, partner in M. M. Warburg & Co. and German financial negotiator at the Paris Peace Conference

stops.name: Trianon Palace, the draft handed over
stops.date_confidence: the handover of the draft treaty at the Trianon Palace on 7 May 1919 and Brockdorff-Rantzau's seated reply are uncontested and documented in the US Foreign Relations series. Warburg's presence as an expert follows from the 12 March appointment; his private judgment of the scene comes from the dossier [R]. Coordinates corrected to the Nominatim geocode of the Trianon Palace, about 1.6 km east of the pair in the research pool.
stops.campa: The Allies hand the draft treaty to the German delegation in the dining room of the Trianon Palace. Brockdorff-Rantzau, the foreign minister, answers from his chair without standing, and every man in the room who is not German reads it as contempt. Warburg is present as an expert. His judgment, set down afterwards, is that the reply was an uncoordinated blunder that spent whatever room Germany had left. The delegation goes back to its hotel with a document none of them believes can be paid.
suggested_refs: history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1919Parisv11/d245, on the 7 May 1919 handover
sources: Neue Deutsche Biographie, via the research dossier

stops.name: Versailles, the experts say it cannot be paid
stops.date_confidence: the unanimous expert submission of 18-19 June 1919 is held in the Bundesarchiv (R 43 I/5) and was not refetched this session [R]. The treaty chronology, National Assembly acceptance under ultimatum and signature on 28 June 1919, is attested.
stops.campa: With Wilhelm Cuno and the other financial experts, Warburg signs a unanimous recommendation to the cabinet in Berlin: the reparations and economic terms cannot be met and the treaty should be refused. The National Assembly accepts it regardless, under an ultimatum that hostilities will otherwise resume, and it is signed at Versailles on the twenty-eighth of June. His opposition to the economic terms is on the record before the signature. That will turn out to protect him from nothing.
suggested_refs: Bundesarchiv R 43 I/5, the German delegation's expert submissions of June 1919

stops.name: Berlin, the Deutsche Warentreuhand
stops.date_confidence: attested; de.wiki records the Deutsche Warentreuhand AG initiative with Paul von Mendelssohn-Bartholdy in 1920 and the founding of the Übersee-Club in Hamburg in 1922. Months and days unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: German firms need foreign credit and have no collateral a foreign lender will accept, because the collateral sits inside Germany and Germany has just lost. With Paul von Mendelssohn-Bartholdy, Warburg sets up the Deutsche Warentreuhand: goods are transferred in trust to the company, which holds title for the foreign lender, and the loan follows the title. It is a lawyer's device that lets a defeated economy borrow against goods nobody abroad can seize. Two years later he founds the Übersee-Club in Hamburg, a dining club for the overseas trade.
suggested_refs: The Deutsche Warentreuhand AG and fiduciary title transfer in postwar German foreign borrowing
The Übersee-Club, Hamburg, founded 1922

stops.name: Edmund-Siemers-Allee, the university he argued for
stops.date_confidence: the honorary doctorate of 1921 and the Hamburg Chamber of Commerce gold medal of 1927 are both listed by deutsche-biographie (NDB) [A]. The 1907 foundation of the Hamburgische Wissenschaftliche Stiftung, the 1908 Colonial Institute and Warburg's part in the university campaign come from the NDB and Bajohr [R]. The 1921 honorary life membership of the Verein für Hamburgische Geschichte and its 1938 revocation are recorded by de.wiki. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Hamburg is the richest city in Germany without a university, and its merchants have long preferred it so. Warburg works with senator Werner von Melle for fourteen years to change that: the Hamburgische Wissenschaftliche Stiftung in 1907, the Colonial Institute in 1908, and at last, in the republic's first year, a full university. In 1921 it gives him an honorary doctorate. The same year the Verein für Hamburgische Geschichte makes him an honorary member for life. In 1938 it takes that back.
suggested_refs: The Hamburgische Wissenschaftliche Stiftung (1907) and the founding of the University of Hamburg (1919)
sources: Frank Bajohr, 'Das Jüdische Hamburg', via the research dossier

stops.name: Königsallee, the car in the Grunewald
stops.date_confidence: Rathenau's assassination on 24 June 1922 is attested. The reported plans of the same milieu against Warburg come from the NDB and the Hoffmann biography and were not independently confirmed this session [R]. Coordinates corrected to the memorial site near Koenigsallee 65, about 550 m west of the pair in the research pool; Nominatim returns no result for the memorial itself, so this is the best available fix rather than a fetched authority.
stops.campa: Walther Rathenau, foreign minister, industrialist, Jew, is shot in his open car on the Königsallee on the way to the ministry. The men who do it belong to Organisation Consul, and when the police work through what else that circle had been preparing, Warburg's name is on a list. He does not leave Germany, and he does not stop travelling to Berlin, and no guard is mentioned in anything he wrote. He is fifty-five years old. The threats stay threats for another eleven years.
suggested_refs: The Rathenau memorial on the Koenigsallee, Grunewald, Berlin
sources: Neue Deutsche Biographie, via the research dossier
Gabriele Hoffmann, 'Max M. Warburg', via the research dossier

stops.name: Berlin, the Reichsbank general council
stops.date_confidence: attested; de.wiki gives the appointment to the eight-member Reichsbankrat in 1924, and dasjuedischehamburg confirms the general council role, running to 1933. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinates are the Reichsbank complex at Jägerstraße.
stops.campa: The Dawes settlement rebuilds the Reichsbank as an institution under foreign supervision, and Warburg is appointed to its Generalrat, the general council of eight, which meets in the Reichsbank on the Jägerstraße. The mark has been stabilized. American money is arriving on short terms and being lent long, and the men in this room understand what that means and take it anyway, because the alternative is no money at all. He keeps the seat until 1933.
suggested_refs: The Reichsbank Generalrat under the Dawes Plan, 1924-1933

stops.name: Hamburg, the libel suit against Fritsch
stops.date_confidence: the trial and the conviction are attested by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency of 8 December 1924 and by TIME of 15 December 1924; the hearing dates of 4-5 December follow the research pool. Fritsch's appeal was heard by the Hamburg Court of Appeals in October 1926 (JTA, 20 October 1926). His 'Mein Streit mit dem Hause Warburg' is catalogued by Open Library as first published 1925; the place of publication, given as Leipzig in the pool, is not carried by that record.
stops.campa: Theodor Fritsch, publishing antisemitica since the 1880s, prints the charge that Warburg and Melchior served Allied interests at Versailles and betrayed Germany there. The two men sue him for libel in Hamburg. Warburg testifies, is cross-examined on the entire imagined architecture of international Jewish finance, and tells the court it cannot be proved because there is nothing there to prove. He adds that German Jews have been good advisers to the state in emergencies, and names Bleichröder, who advised Bismarck. Fritsch is convicted and sentenced to three months.
stops.quote: the international dictatorship of Jewish high finance can never be proved because it does not exist.
stops.quote_source: Max Warburg's courtroom testimony, reported in TIME, 'Germany: Anti-Semitic,' 15 December 1924
suggested_refs: Theodor Fritsch, 'Mein Streit mit dem Hause Warburg' (1925), the defendant's own printing of the case record
sources: Open Library record for Theodor Fritsch, 'Mein Streit mit dem Hause Warburg'

stops.name: Frankfurt, the seat on the I.G. Farben board
stops.date_confidence: de.wiki gives the supervisory-board tenure precisely as 1925-1931; month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinates are the Nominatim geocode of the I.G.-Farben-Haus and are anachronistic for the start of the tenure, since that building was completed only in 1930 and no earlier board address was located; the pair in the research pool was a further 350 m off.
stops.campa: He takes a seat on the supervisory board of I.G. Farben, the chemical combine assembled the year before out of six firms, and holds it until 1931. That is the whole of it. The company's later name is written on Auschwitz and has nothing to do with this seat, which ends two years before the seizure of power and belongs to a Weimar board of a Weimar company. The headquarters that now stands for the combine in every photograph is not finished until 1930, five years after he joins it.
suggested_refs: wollheim-memorial.de, on I.G. Farben's conduct in the Nazi period, well after Warburg's tenure ended
sources: Neue Deutsche Biographie, via the research dossier

stops.name: Ferdinandstraße 75, the year the banks fail
stops.date_confidence: the 1929 balance sheet of 382 million marks and 289 employees is given by mmwarburg.de. The bank's survival without direct state rescue and the Kuhn, Loeb support are carried from the research pool's secondary synthesis [R]. The 1931 departure from the German People's Party is widely repeated in German biographical summaries but was not confirmed in either encyclopedia article fetched [R]. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The Danatbank fails and the German banking system goes down with it. The great universal banks are rescued by the state and effectively nationalized. M. M. Warburg & Co. comes through without a direct state rescue. It had 289 employees and a balance sheet of 382 million marks in 1929, it lends conservatively, and when the run reaches Hamburg millions arrive from Kuhn, Loeb in New York, where Paul Warburg's half of the family has been for a generation. The same year Max leaves the German People's Party as it turns against the republic.
suggested_refs: The German banking crisis of July 1931 and the collapse of the Danatbank
sources: Christopher Kopper, via the research dossier

stops.name: Ballindamm, the farewell nobody offers him
stops.date_confidence: summer 1933 per the biographical accounts; month set to July and day to 01 to order the segment, neither being attested. The wording of the speech survives through Hoffmann's biography and family transmission of the text, not a contemporaneous transcript [R].
stops.campa: He is put off the HAPAG supervisory board after twenty-three years on it, and no colleague stands up to say anything, so he says it himself, in the third person, to the men sitting there. The great and mighty German merchant marine, he tells them, is chiefly the work of two Jews: one of them Albert Ballin, dead since 1918, and the other the man who has the honour to stand before them. Then he takes the board's own voice and accepts, on its behalf, the blame for dismissing a proven colleague.
stops.quote: Die große und mächtige deutsche Schifffahrt ist vornehmlich das Werk zweier Juden. Der eine ist der verstorbene Albert Ballin und der andere ist der Mann, der die Ehre hat, vor Ihnen zu stehen.
stops.quote_source: Max Warburg's farewell address on his removal from the HAPAG supervisory board, 1933, quoted in Gabriele Hoffmann, 'Max M. Warburg' (Ellert & Richter, Hamburg 2009), cited in the German Wikipedia article 'Max Warburg'
suggested_refs: The HAPAG boardroom on the Ballindamm, and the 1933 purge of Jewish supervisory board members

stops.name: Ferdinandstraße 75, the transfer structure
stops.date_confidence: 1933 is attested for the Haavara agreement generally. Warburg's and Melchior's role in negotiating the transfer structure, and the bank's own Paltreu and Alltreu vehicles, come from the research pool's citation of Avraham Barkai, 'German Interests in the Ha'avara-Transfer Agreement', Leo Baeck Institute Year Book 35 (1990) [R]. Month and day defaulted to 01. The quotation dates from a speech of July 1935 and is placed here for its subject, not its date.
stops.campa: German Jews may leave and may not take their money out. Warburg and Melchior work on the structure that becomes the Haavara: the emigrant deposits his assets in Germany, the deposit buys German goods, the goods are sold in Mandatory Palestine, and he receives value there after deductions. The bank runs its own vehicles, Paltreu and Alltreu, on the same principle. It moves people out of Germany. It earns Germany foreign exchange. Both of those are true.
stops.quote: Palestine cannot absorb all Jewish emigrants, even if the number of Jews which it took in the past year was much larger than anyone expected.
stops.quote_source: Max Warburg, address on the Hilfsverein der deutschen Juden, reported by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, 2 July 1935
suggested_refs: Avraham Barkai, 'German Interests in the Ha'avara-Transfer Agreement', Leo Baeck Institute Year Book 35 (1990)

stops.name: Hamburg harbour, the library sails
stops.date_confidence: the shipment of 12 December 1933 is attested. Max Warburg's authorization and financing are asserted by the dossier and by the English Wikipedia article on Aby Warburg, but the Warburg Institute's own published history credits the removal to Lord Lee of Fareham, Samuel Courtauld and the Warburg family collectively; his personal role is therefore carried as [R]. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the existing Hamburg harbour pin for the same shipment.
stops.campa: Aby Warburg has been dead four years and his library is a hostage: the books, the photographic collection, the papers, and the staff who know how the shelving works. Fritz Saxl arranges the removal to London and Max, who has been paying for the thing since he was twelve years old, backs it and signs for it. The crates go out of the harbour on the twelfth of December, the books, the photographs and the papers together. It is the last draw on an account opened by a promise to a thirteen-year-old boy.
stops.quote_source: Max Warburg on the promise to his brother Aby, quoted in Karen Michels, 'Es muss besser werden!' (Hamburg University Press, 2020)
suggested_refs: The Kulturwissenschaftliche Bibliothek Warburg and its removal from Hamburg to London, December 1933
sources: warburg.sas.ac.uk, 'History of the Warburg Institute' (HTTP 403 on direct fetch this session)

stops.name: Hamburg, the chair of the Hilfsverein
stops.date_confidence: the sources conflict on when the chairmanship began and the conflict is left standing: deutsche-biographie (NDB) says he became chairman of the Hilfsverein der deutschen Juden in 1928, de.wiki gives 1935-1938. The JTA obituary confirms the role and his father's part in founding the organization. Month and day defaulted to 01. His seat on the Jewish Agency advisory council for Germany in 1929 comes from the research dossier alone; no fetched source and no existing journey file confirms it [R].
stops.campa: He chairs the Hilfsverein der deutschen Juden, the relief and emigration organization his own father helped found, and it is now the machinery by which German Jews get out: visas, ship tickets, foreign currency, destination countries that keep closing one after another. He sits too on the German advisory council of the Jewish Agency, the Zionist and non-Zionist coalition Chaim Weizmann assembled in 1929, and says the cooperation of the two camps in the emigration work has been exemplary. He is sixty-eight.
stops.quote: What I feel hardest among the many hardships which have broken over us in these last few years, is that even such a time of the hardest trial has not united the German Jews as it obviously should in one single task, in one single idea: How can we best help our co-sufferers?
stops.quote_source: Max Warburg, address on the Hilfsverein der deutschen Juden, reported by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, 2 July 1935
suggested_refs: The Hilfsverein der deutschen Juden and German Jewish emigration finance, 1933-1938

stops.name: Hartungstraße, the Jewish Community House opens
stops.date_confidence: attested in full by keydocuments.net (source jgo:source-118): the opening on 9 January 1938, Warburg's financial and personal backing, his advocacy for the Jewish Cultural Association against the German-Israelite Congregation, the six-and-a-half-page typescript address, and its holding in the Max M. Warburg Collection at the Leo Baeck Institute, New York. Coordinates corrected to the Nominatim geocode of Hartungstraße 9-11.
stops.campa: On the ninth of January he opens the Jewish Community House at Hartungstraße 9 to 11 in Rotherbaum, which he has paid for and argued for against the congregation's own board. The Jewish Cultural Association has been shut out of every other hall in the city and now has one of its own. His opening address runs to six and a half typed pages and survives in his papers in New York. He is seventy. He has four months left in the bank, and the building is still standing today, in use as a theatre.
suggested_refs: keydocuments.net/source/jgo:source-118, Warburg's opening address, Max M. Warburg Collection, Leo Baeck Institute, New York
The Hamburger Kammerspiele at Hartungstraße 9-11, the building today

stops.name: Ferdinandstraße 75, farewell to two hundred employees
stops.date_confidence: May 1938 is attested by de.wiki and en.wiki for his departure and the transfer of the partnership to Rudolf Brinckmann and Paul Wirtz; day defaulted to 01. The wording of the farewell survives through Eckart Klessmann's 1998 history of the bank and family transmission, not a contemporaneous transcript [R].
stops.campa: The Aryanization is finished in May. The partnership passes to Rudolf Brinckmann and Paul Wirtz, two non-Jewish men Warburg has chosen himself, because they are the only kind of successor now available and because he trusts them. The house has been in the family since 1798, a hundred and forty years, and this is the fifth year of the government that has just finished taking it. He says goodbye to the roughly two hundred employees still there, and wishes their work success, for the blessing of the Hanseatic City of Hamburg and for the blessing of Germany.
stops.quote: Wir wünschen Ihrer Arbeit Erfolg, zum Segen der Hansestadt Hamburg und zum Segen Deutschlands.
stops.quote_source: Max Warburg's farewell address to the remaining employees of M. M. Warburg & Co., May 1938, quoted in Eckart Klessmann's 1998 history of the bank, cited in the German Wikipedia article 'Max Warburg'
suggested_refs: Eckart Klessmann, history of M. M. Warburg & Co. (1998), source of the farewell text

segments.name: New York, and the Name Returned

stops.name: New York, the crossing at seventy-one
stops.date_confidence: the August 1938 emigration is attested by both Wikipedia articles, by businessofemancipation.org and by dasjuedischehamburg; day defaulted to 01. Fritz Moritz Warburg's arrest, months of detention and eventual settlement in Stockholm are recorded by the English Wikipedia article on M. M. Warburg & Co., which also calls him the bank's former head; that is wrong, Max led the firm from 1910 to 1938 and Fritz was a partner. Coordinates are a Manhattan city pin.
stops.campa: He arrives in the United States in late August with Alice and a daughter, seventy-one years old, formerly the head of a Hamburg house that no longer carries his name. In November the synagogues burn and his younger brother Fritz, a partner in the firm, is arrested and held for months before he is let out of Germany to Stockholm, where he takes Swedish citizenship. Whatever thought there had been of going back does not survive that news. He speaks the language of the country he has landed in because he learned it at a desk in the City of London fifty years earlier. He never sees Hamburg again.
suggested_refs: The Max M. Warburg Collection, Leo Baeck Institute, New York

stops.name: New York, the oath at seventy-seven
stops.date_confidence: attested; deutsche-biographie and the English Wikipedia article both give the naturalization as 1944. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinates are a Manhattan city pin; no residence address was established.
stops.campa: At seventy-seven he becomes a citizen of the United States. He was born a subject of the North German Confederation in its first year and has outlived it, the empire that replaced it, and the republic that replaced that. The oath is taken in the city his brother Paul went to a generation earlier, and where Kuhn, Loeb has been carrying Warburg paper for half a century, so that the family's American half is now simply the family. What he said about it that day, if he said anything, is not recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: Warburg's 1944 naturalization, recorded in the Neue Deutsche Biographie entry

stops.name: Kösterberg, the house given away
stops.date_confidence: attested by the JTA obituary, which records the 1945 offer, the Nazi seizure and postwar return of the estate, the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee as recipient, and the figure of 200 orphaned children up to the age of sixteen. Month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinates corrected to the Nominatim geocode of Kösterbergstraße, Blankenese. Warburg himself was in New York throughout.
stops.campa: The Nazi state seized the Kösterberg estate and liberation gives it back. Max and Fritz, both out of Germany, give it away again: to the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee, for children up to the age of sixteen who came out of the camps with nobody left. The offer goes by letter from New York in 1945, the first year the post runs again, and he never travels over to see it done. Two hundred of them are housed on the Elbe slope where the family kept its summers from 1899, in the rooms his own children grew up in, above the river traffic.
suggested_refs: The American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee's children's home at Kösterberg, Blankenese, from 1945

stops.name: New York, the death and the funeral
stops.date_confidence: 26 December 1946 is given by deutsche-biographie, de.wiki and en.wiki. The JTA obituary gives 29 December and is the lone outlier; the discrepancy is recorded here, not resolved. The funeral at Park Avenue Synagogue, 50 East 87th Street, is attested by that obituary, and would be more precisely pinned at 40.7811, -73.9579.
stops.campa: He dies in New York at seventy-nine, eight years out of Germany, two years an American. The funeral is at the Park Avenue Synagogue. The wire obituary calls him a banker, a philanthropist and a Jewish communal leader, and puts the emigration of 1938 and the naturalization of 1944 in its opening lines. It also gives the date of his death as the twenty-ninth of December, which is not what any German record says, and the discrepancy has never been reconciled.
suggested_refs: Park Avenue Synagogue, 50 East 87th Street, New York, site of the funeral

stops.name: Sleepy Hollow, the grave the reference works do not record
stops.date_confidence: the burial at Sleepy Hollow Cemetery is stated by the JTA obituary and by no reference work: de.wiki, en.wiki and Wikidata (Q67580, property P119) all leave the burial place blank, checked directly this session. The date follows the funeral and is an inference, not an attested date. Coordinates corrected to the Nominatim geocode of Sleepy Hollow Cemetery; the pair in the research pool fell on the adjacent Old Dutch Church burying ground, which is a legally distinct graveyard.
stops.campa: He is buried at Sleepy Hollow, in Westchester County, thirty miles up the Hudson from the pier he came in through eight years earlier and an ocean from the Ohlsdorf ground in Hamburg where the family's stones stand in a row under the name Warburg. Neither Wikipedia article on him records a burial place, and the Wikidata field for it is empty. The one source that states any burial place at all is the wire obituary printed the week he died, which gives Sleepy Hollow in four words and moves on to the next paragraph.
suggested_refs: The Warburg family graves at the Jüdischer Friedhof Ohlsdorf, Ilandkoppel, Hamburg

stops.name: Warburgstraße, the street in Rotherbaum
stops.date_confidence: attested; de.wiki records the 1947 naming of the Warburgstraße in Rotherbaum. Month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinates corrected to the Nominatim geocode of Warburgstraße; the research pool carried two different pairs for this street, 53.5665, 9.9847 and 53.5661, 9.9871, both wrong by roughly 700 m and disagreeing with each other.
stops.campa: A year after his death Hamburg names a street for him in Rotherbaum, a short walk from the villa at the Mittelweg the family moved into in 1871. This is the same city that struck his honorary membership from its own historical society in 1938 and cleared him out of the Chamber of Commerce he had sat in for thirty-one years, and that let the bank drop his name from its door in 1941. Nobody in it asked him to come back while he was alive. The sign goes up in 1947. He has been dead since the previous December.
suggested_refs: Warburgstraße, Hamburg-Rotherbaum, named 1947
sources: Frank Bajohr, 'Das Jüdische Hamburg', via the research dossier

stops.name: Ferdinandstraße 75, the name comes back in stages
stops.date_confidence: the renaming to Brinckmann, Wirtz & Co. on 27 October 1941, the 1949 restitution agreement negotiated for the family by Eric M. Warburg, the 1969 return of the Warburg name in M.M.Warburg-Brinckmann, Wirtz & Co. and the 1991 adoption of the short form are all given by mmwarburg.de's corporate history and by de.wiki. The English Wikipedia article on the bank states the name remained unchanged through Aryanization, which contradicts both and is recorded here as an outlier to be discarded. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The firm had been renamed Brinckmann, Wirtz & Co. in October 1941, the last of the name gone from the door. In 1949 a restitution agreement makes the Warburgs shareholders again, negotiated for the family by Eric M. Warburg. The name itself returns in stages: M.M.Warburg-Brinckmann, Wirtz & Co. in 1969, and the short form in 1991, forty-five years after Max's death and a hundred and ninety-three after two brothers opened the house. The bank is still at Ferdinandstraße 75.
suggested_refs: mmwarburg.de/en/the-bank/history/, the firm's own chronology of the 1941 renaming and the 1949 restitution
